titre: The Assize of Clarendon (1166): A Jury to Accuse, Water to Decide
accroche: In 1166, Henry II has twelve men per hundred swear to denounce known thieves and murderers. The jurors accuse; the water ordeal ordinarily decides.
contenu_vulgarise:
We readily associate the jury with protection: ordinary citizens standing between the accused and power. One of the texts in which a jury appears in English law, the Assize of Clarendon of 1166, says something else. Henry II decrees there, “by the counsel of all his barons, for the preservation of peace and the keeping of justice,” an inquiry in every county. In each hundred, twelve of the “more lawful men,” and in each township four, must swear to speak the truth: is there among them anyone who, since the king has been king, has been accused or publicly known as a robber, murderer, or thief, or who has harbored one?

These jurors do not judge. Under article 2, the person their oath names “shall go to the ordeal of water”: he goes to the water ordeal and swears that he has been neither a robber, nor a murderer, nor a harborer of such men. The group of neighbors supplies the accusation, and the ordeal stands in for the decision. The assize nonetheless provides for cases where it is refused: the notorious suspect caught with the stolen goods and without a guarantor is not entitled to it (article 12), nor is the man who confessed before lawful men or in the hundred court, then wished to retract (article 13).

## A tool of the king

The text does not protect the accused; it organizes the king's takeover of law enforcement. Article 8 requires everyone to come and take this oath at the county courts, with no privilege excusing anyone from coming. Article 5 says that, for those taken on this oath, no one but the king shall have court, justice, or chattels: the king keeps all their movable goods. Article 7 has prisons built, at the king's expense, in the counties that lack them.

Even a successful ordeal does not always set a man free. According to article 14, a man “absolved by the law” at the ordeal, but of very bad reputation and publicly defamed by the testimony of many men, must abjure the king's lands: he must cross the sea within eight days, unless the wind holds him back, and never return to England without the king's mercy. If he returns, he is an outlaw. Article 22 specifies that the assize will be observed as long as it pleases the king.

## What this shifts

Wikipedia ranks these twelve men among the prototypes of the *grand jury*, which in theory only brings accusations without establishing guilt. It adds that some historians trace the beginnings of the jury to before this act. The jury that judges will come later: the 1166 text does not provide for it.

We therefore often take for a conquest by the subjects against the prince a device born of the prince's need: to learn, from those who live next door, who passes for a thief in each village. The jury of 1166 questions neighbors on the king's behalf.

That the same group of neighbors ended up judging, and no longer merely accusing, is another story, one the assize does not tell.

carte.punch: The jury of 1166 did not judge: it denounced. The verdict, as a rule, fell to the water ordeal.
carte.idee: In the Assize of Clarendon (1166), twelve men per hundred swear to name known thieves and murderers. The accused then goes to the water ordeal, and even if acquitted, if his reputation is very bad, he must leave the kingdom within eight days.

quiz.question: In the Assize of Clarendon (1166), what ordinarily happens when the twelve men's oath names a suspect?
choix: The twelve men deliberate separately and return a verdict of guilt
The suspect goes to the water ordeal and swears he has been neither a robber nor a murderer
The suspect is released on bail pending a trial before his peers
The suspect is banished from the kingdom within eight days without further process
quiz.explication: The twelve men's oath serves as the accusation. The suspect then goes to the water ordeal and swears his innocence (article 2), except in the cases where the ordeal is refused (articles 12 and 13). Banishment within eight days (article 14) strikes only the man absolved at the ordeal but of very bad reputation, and the text does not entrust the twelve men with judging.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which case does the Assize of Clarendon refuse the water ordeal to the accused?
choix: If he is accused by fewer than twelve men of the hundred
If he refuses to post bail before judgment
If he confessed and then retracted before the hundred court
If he has already been tried by an ecclesiastical court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 13 refuses the ordeal to anyone who confessed before lawful men or the hundred court and then retracted; article 12 also excludes the suspect caught with the stolen goods, without a guarantor. Bail and an ecclesiastical court are absent from the text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to article 5 of the Assize of Clarendon, what becomes of the property of a man taken on the twelve men's oath?
choix: It is divided among the twelve jurors who accused him
It goes to the king, who keeps all his movable goods
It is handed over to the Church for the duration of his detention
It stays with his family until the ordeal's outcome
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 5 says that no one but the king shall have court, justice, or chattels over the man the oath names: the king keeps all his movable goods. The text provides neither for a division among jurors, nor for a handover to the Church, nor for the property staying with the family.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to article 14, what must a man absolved at the ordeal but of very bad reputation do?
choix: Pay a fine to the county that tried him
Appear each year before the county court
Hand over his property to the juror who denounced him
Leave the kingdom within eight days, unless the wind is against him
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 14 requires him to abjure the king's lands: cross the sea within eight days, unless the wind holds him back, and not return without the king's mercy, on pain of being an outlaw. A fine, an annual appearance, and a transfer to a juror appear nowhere in it.
